questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count carbon groups on the alcohol carbon
questions.stem: From the numbers, a Grignard reagent adds to acetone. How many carbon groups are attached to the carbinol carbon in the resulting alcohol?
questions.explanation: Acetone has two methyl groups on the carbonyl carbon and the Grignard adds a third carbon group, so after workup the carbinol carbon bears three carbon substituents and is a tertiary alcohol.
questions.hint: Two original groups plus one added group.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: From the numbers, how many atoms are in the ring of an epoxide?
questions.explanation: An epoxide is a three-membered cyclic ether containing two carbons and one oxygen, and its strain drives ring-opening reactions with nucleophiles.
questions.hint: Epoxides are three-membered rings.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count oxygen atoms in the product
questions.stem: From the numbers, oxidation of a secondary alcohol with PCC gives a ketone. How many oxygen atoms does the ketone product contain?
questions.explanation: A ketone contains a single carbonyl oxygen, since oxidation of a secondary alcohol removes two hydrogens and forms a carbon-oxygen double bond without adding a second oxygen.
questions.hint: A ketone has one carbonyl oxygen.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: From the numbers, ethanol has a pKa near 16 and ethanethiol near 10.5. By about how many pKa units is the thiol more acidic?
questions.explanation: Subtracting 10.5 from 16 gives about 5.5 pKa units, meaning ethanethiol is roughly 5.5 orders of magnitude more acidic than ethanol.
questions.hint: Subtract the pKa values.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: From the numbers, hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene gives predominantly how many constitutional alcohol products?
questions.explanation: Hydroboration of this alkene is highly regioselective for the less substituted carbon, so predominantly one constitutional alcohol product forms, though as a racemate if a stereocenter is generated.
questions.hint: Regioselectivity gives one constitutional product.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: From the numbers, cleavage of one mole of diethyl ether with excess HBr yields how many moles of ethyl bromide?
questions.explanation: Both ethyl groups of the ether are converted to ethyl bromide under excess HBr, so one mole of ether gives two moles of ethyl bromide and one mole of water.
questions.hint: Each ethyl group becomes a bromide.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does epoxide opening occur at different carbons under acidic versus basic conditions?

answer.exemplar: Under basic conditions the nucleophile attacks the less hindered carbon in an SN2-like process because sterics dominate; under acidic conditions protonation gives the epoxide carbocation character concentrated at the more substituted carbon, which can better stabilize positive charge, so electronic effects dominate and attack occurs there.

questions.explanation: Steric control in base, electronic control in acid. Under basic conditions the nucleophile attacks the less hindered carbon in an SN2-like process because sterics dominate; under acidic conditions protonation gives the epoxide carbocation character concentrated at the more substituted carbon, which can better stabilize positive charge, so electronic effects dominate and attack occurs there.
questions.hint: Compare the transition states.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why can aqueous chromic acid oxidize a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid while PCC stops at the aldehyde?

answer.exemplar: Aqueous chromic acid forms a hydrate of the aldehyde in the presence of water, and that hydrate is further oxidized to the acid; PCC is used under anhydrous conditions, so the aldehyde hydrate cannot form and oxidation stops at the aldehyde stage.

questions.hint: Presence or absence of water is decisive.

questions.stem: Explain the following: why must Grignard reactions be carried out under strictly anhydrous conditions?

questions.stem: Explain the following: why is ethanethiol more acidic than ethanol even though sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen?

answer.exemplar: The conjugate base of a thiol places negative charge on sulfur, which is larger and more polarizable than oxygen and can spread the charge over a greater volume, so the thiolate is better stabilized than an alkoxide and its parent acid is stronger.

questions.hint: Electronegativity is not the only factor.

questions.stem: Discuss the reasoning: why can aqueous chromic acid oxidize a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid while PCC stops at the aldehyde?

questions.learningObjective: Explain the need for dry conditions
questions.stem: Discuss the reasoning: why must Grignard reactions be carried out under strictly anhydrous conditions?

answer.exemplar: The carbon-magnesium bond is highly polar and makes the carbon strongly basic, so any water, alcohol or acid present would protonate the Grignard reagent and destroy it, forming an alkane instead of adding to the intended carbonyl.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Discuss the reasoning: why is ethanethiol more acidic than ethanol even though sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen?

answer.exemplar: The conjugate base of a thiol places negative charge on sulfur, which is larger and more polarizable than oxygen and can spread the charge over a greater volume, so the thiolate is better stabilized than an alkoxide and its parent acid is stronger.
